summary: This unit teaches you to plan, prepare, plate and store desserts for a villa or hotel: whipping cream and meringue, set desserts with gelatine, custards and sauces, chocolate and sugar, frozen and fruit desserts, and Jamaican favourites such as sweet potato pudding and gizzada. You will also learn to present desserts attractively, control portions and keep them safe for guests with allergies and special diets.

blocks.p: This unit covers the dessert course of a villa dinner, a hotel lunch or a buffet, from the standard recipe to the plate in front of the guest. It is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. A dessert is the last thing the guest remembers about a meal, so it must look good, taste good and, above all, be **safe**.

Desserts use many skills at once: baking, whisking, setting, cooking sauces, working with chocolate and sugar, and plating. They also carry the highest food safety risks in the kitchen, because cream, custard and mousse are ideal places for germs to grow, and because many guests have allergies or special diets.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's kitchen. In practical work you prepare and plate a hot dessert (bread pudding with crème anglaise) and a cold dessert (meringue nests with cream, fruit and coulis). The assessor watches your planning, safety, allergen care, method, plating and clean-up as well as the taste.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the food, your hands and the work area. Do not photograph a person's face unless they agree and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Mise en place for a dessert course

blocks.p: **Mise en place** means having everything in its place before you start. For a dessert course for a villa dinner, work through these steps:

flow: Check the menu, the number of guests and any allergies or special diets
Read the standard recipe for every part of the dessert
Scale the recipe for the number of portions, plus one or two spare
Write a list of ingredients and equipment; check stock and dates
Make a time plan: what is made first, what needs time to set, what is left to the last minute
Weigh and measure every ingredient
Preheat the oven; prepare tins, moulds, piping bags and garnishes
Chill the plates for cold desserts, and warm them for hot ones

ul: A mousse is made hours ahead so that it can set. A sauce is made earlier and chilled. Fruit is cut close to service, so that it stays fresh.
Take out of the fridge only what you need, and put it back.
Weigh baking ingredients in grams. Baking needs exact amounts to work.
Tell the chef at once if something is missing.
Every food handler in Jamaica must hold a **Food Handler's Permit** from the local health department.
Wear a clean uniform and apron; cover all your hair; keep nails short; take off jewellery and watches.
**Wash your hands** with soap and warm water before starting, after handling raw egg, after touching your face, hair or phone, and after the toilet.
Cover cuts with a blue waterproof plaster and a glove. Tell your supervisor if you are ill.
Use clean tools and wash, rinse and sanitise between jobs. Use clean tasting spoons: never lick a spoon and put it back.

head: Job
Typical figure
Why
rows: Storing fresh cream, custard, mousse, cream gateau
Germs grow slowly in the cold.
Germs multiply fastest. Keep cream desserts out of it, as the Centre's food safety plan says.
Ice cream and sorbet in the freezer

blocks.note: These are the usual teaching figures. Follow the Centre's food safety plan and your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Use clean eggs with no cracks, within their date. Crack them on a flat surface into a cup, not on the edge of the bowl.
Desserts such as mousse and some meringues use **uncooked** or lightly cooked egg. Use **pasteurised** egg for these, because raw egg can carry salmonella.
Desserts with **cream, custard, mousse or fresh fruit** are high-risk foods. They must be covered, labelled, kept in the fridge and used in date order.
Do not keep desserts that have stood out at room temperature longer than the Centre's plan allows; throw them away.

head: Allergen or diet
Where it hides in desserts
What to do
rows: Garnishes (cashew, almond), praline, marzipan, chocolate, biscuits, ice cream
Check every label, including 'may contain nuts' warnings; keep nuts off the plate.
Flour, cakes, biscuits, pastry, thickened sauces, some chocolate
Use a gluten-free flour or choose a fruit dessert.
Cream, butter, custard, ice cream, chocolate
List it; offer a sorbet or a dairy-free dessert.
Use agar, a plant-based setting agent.
Guest who eats no pork or alcohol
Lard in pastry, gelatine from pork, rum in puddings

ul: If you are not sure whether a dessert contains an allergen, **check the recipe and the labels, or ask the chef**. Never guess: an allergic reaction can be serious.

Make the allergy-free dessert **first**, on a cleaned and sanitised surface, with clean tools and bowls and clean piping bags. Keep it covered, apart from other desserts, and label it with the guest's name.
Serve it straight to the right guest, and tell the guest what it is.

head: Hazard
How you prevent harm
rows: Keep the guard on; start on a low speed
Switch off and wait for it to stop before you scrape the bowl or change the attachment
Heavy pan, handle turned in, long spoon; never leave it
Hot sugar sticks to skin and burns deeply: never touch or taste it
Add liquid carefully, because it spits
Lift lids away from you; carry a bain-marie level.
Use a sharp knife on a board that does not slip; carry it point down.

blocks.note: Cool a burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes. Do not use ice, butter or toothpaste. Report every burn and write it in the accident book.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Scrape
Wash with hot water and detergent
Rinse
Sanitise
Dry

blocks.p: Clean work surfaces after every dessert, and never wipe with the cloth that was used for raw food. Switch off and unplug the mixer before cleaning.
Sifting flour or icing sugar **removes lumps and adds air**. Sift icing sugar before you use it for dusting or icing.

ul: Use **chilled whipping cream or heavy cream** (a cream with enough fat, usually about 35% or more) in a cold, clean bowl. Cream with too little fat will not whip.
Whisk steadily. At first the cream thickens; **soft peaks** are enough for folding into a mousse. Stop at **firm peaks** for piping.
**Over-whipped cream** turns grainy and starts to turn into butter. It cannot be piped smoothly. If it begins to go grainy, stop at once and fold in a spoonful of fresh cream.
Whip close to service and keep it chilled at 5 °C or below.

flow: Separate the eggs with care: no yolk in the whites
Use a very clean, grease-free bowl and whisk
Whisk the whites until foamy
Add the sugar **gradually**, a spoonful at a time, whisking all the time
Whisk until thick, glossy and holding stiff peaks
Pipe or spoon onto lined trays
Bake in a very low oven, about 100–120 °C as the recipe says, until crisp and dry
Leave to cool in the oven or on a rack; store dry in an airtight tin

head: Point
Why
rows: Fat stops the whites foaming up.
Add the sugar gradually, once the whites are foamy
Adding it too early or all at once stops the whites reaching full volume, and undissolved sugar makes the meringue weep sugary drops.
Meringue is dried, not baked: a hot oven browns it and makes it chewy or cracked.
Meringue soaks up moisture and goes soft and sticky in humid weather. Store it in an airtight tin.
Cream and fruit make it go soft.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid weather softens meringue fast. Bake it on a dry day if you can, cool it fully before storing, and put in the filling just before the dessert goes out.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Folding** means gently cutting through a mix with a metal spoon or spatula and turning it over, so that the air is not knocked out. Use it when you add flour to a whisked sponge, or whipped cream or egg whites to a mousse.

ul: Many desserts use a sponge or cake base. In the creaming method, beat **butter and sugar** together until pale and fluffy, then add the eggs a **little at a time** so that the mix does not curdle (split).
Test a sponge with a skewer: it should come out clean, and the top should spring back when pressed.
Preheat the oven so that the cake starts baking at the right heat.

blocks.p: Many desserts sit on a pastry base. You need the basics of short pastry and choux, which are covered more fully in the pastry unit.

ul: Rub cold fat into flour until it looks like fine breadcrumbs, add a little cold water (or egg for a sweet pastry), and handle it as little as possible.
**Rest** it in the fridge: this firms the fat and stops shrinking.
Handling and kneading it too much makes it **tough and hard**.
Roll it evenly, lift it into the tin without stretching, prick the base, and rest it again.
**Bake blind** (lined with paper and baking beans) for a wet filling such as pastry cream, then fill and decorate.

blocks.p: Choux is cooked in a pan from water, butter and flour, then beaten with eggs, piped and baked until it puffs into a hollow shell. It makes **éclairs and profiteroles**. Fill with chilled cream or pastry cream just before service, because filled shells go soft and the cream must stay cold.

ul: Made from milk, egg yolks, sugar, flour or cornflour and vanilla; boiled and stirred until thick.
Cool it quickly in a shallow tray covered with film touching the surface, and chill it at 5 °C or below.

blocks.note: Fresh fruit tarts are best finished close to service. A thin glaze over the fruit makes it shine. Dust icing sugar over a moist tart **just before it goes to the guest**, or it will melt into the fruit.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Agent
What it is
How to use it
Notes
rows: Leaf: soak in cold water until soft, squeeze out the water, then melt gently in a little warm liquid
Powder: sprinkle over cold water and leave to swell, then melt gently
**Never boil it**: boiling weakens its setting power. Not suitable for vegetarians.
A setting agent made from seaweed
Boil it in the liquid to dissolve it, then cool
Suitable for **vegetarians**. Sets firmer and at room temperature.
Mix with cold liquid, then cook and stir
Used for thickened puddings and sauces.
Used in baked custards and crème caramel.

blocks.p: Jamaica also has its own seaweed-based thickener, Irish moss, which is boiled to make drinks and puddings. Like agar, it comes from seaweed.

Some **fresh** fruits contain **enzymes** that break down gelatine, so the jelly or mousse will not set. The main ones are **fresh pineapple, papaya (paw-paw) and kiwi fruit**. Cooking the fruit, or using **canned** pineapple, destroys the enzyme, so it can be used safely. Fresh mango, orange, strawberry and passion fruit do not have this problem.

flow: Weigh the ingredients and prepare the moulds or glasses
Soak the leaf gelatine in cold water until soft; squeeze it out
Purée ripe mango and sweeten it
Melt the gelatine gently in a little warm purée, stirring until dissolved: do not boil
Stir the gelatine into the rest of the mango purée
Whip chilled cream to soft peaks and fold it in gently
Fold in pasteurised egg white if the recipe uses it
Pour into moulds, cover, label and chill at 5 °C or below until set, usually several hours
Turn out or serve in the glass, with a garnish just before service

ul: **Why fold the cream in?** Folding keeps the air in, so the mousse is light.
**Why chill for hours?** Gelatine takes time to set. The dessert is made a day ahead if it is for a villa dinner, covered, labelled with the date and chilled.
Test: a set mousse holds its shape when the glass is tilted, and does not run.

head: Dessert
What it is
rows: Fruit juice set with gelatine (or agar), often with pieces of cooked or canned fruit.
Egg custard sauce with gelatine, then whipped cream folded in.
Cream and milk set lightly with gelatine.
Fruit or chocolate with whipped cream (and sometimes egg white) folded in and set.

flow: Heat milk with vanilla to just below boiling
Whisk egg yolks and sugar until pale
Pour a little hot milk onto the yolks, whisking, then add the rest
Pour back into a clean pan and cook over a low heat, stirring all the time
Cook until the sauce **coats the back of a spoon**; a line drawn through it stays clear
Strain into a cold bowl at once
Cool quickly, cover and chill

ul: **Never let it boil.** The egg scrambles and the sauce curdles. Keep the heat low and stir all the time, round the base and edges.
To save a sauce that is just starting to curdle, take it off the heat at once, pour it into a cold bowl and whisk hard. A badly scrambled sauce cannot be saved.
Use it with hot puddings, tarts and cakes.

blocks.p: A **crème caramel** or other baked custard is cooked in a dish standing in a tray of hot water, a **bain-marie**, in a moderate oven. The water makes the heat gentle and even, so the custard sets smoothly, without curdling or bubbles. A crème caramel has a layer of caramel in the bottom of the dish, which melts into a sauce when the dessert is turned out.

head: Baked custard point
Why
rows: Gentle heat, so the custard sets smoothly.
A hot oven curdles the egg.
Take out while it still wobbles slightly in the centre
It finishes setting as it cools.

blocks.p: A **slurry** is cornflour mixed with a little cold water or milk. Stir it into a hot sauce and cook, stirring, until it thickens and loses its raw taste. Never put dry cornflour straight into a hot liquid, because it forms lumps.

ul: A **coulis** is a smooth sauce of puréed fruit, such as mango, guava or passion fruit.
Blend ripe fruit with a little sugar and lime juice. **Pass it through a fine sieve** to take out seeds and fibres, so that it is smooth.
Taste and adjust: add sugar if too sharp, lime juice if too sweet.
Keep it covered in the fridge; use it within the time the Centre's plan allows.
Chop the chocolate and melt it in a clean, dry bowl **over a pan of simmering water**, with the bowl not touching the water. Stir gently.
Do not let the chocolate get too hot: it should stay warm, not hot. Too much heat makes it grainy and dull.
**A drop of water or steam makes chocolate seize**: it turns thick, dull and lumpy. Keep the bowl and spoon completely dry.
Chocolate is fine in a microwave in short bursts, stirring between each.

flow: Put sugar (and a little water) in a clean, heavy pan
Dissolve over a low heat, then boil without stirring until it turns golden
Take it off the heat at once, because it keeps darkening
Use it immediately; add any liquid very carefully, standing back

blocks.note: Hot sugar is far hotter than boiling water and it **sticks to the skin and burns badly**. Use a heavy pan, a long spoon and a handle turned in. Keep a bowl of cold water close to cool a burn, never touch the sugar, and keep children and bystanders away.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Dessert
What it is
Notes
rows: Frozen cream and milk (often egg custard), sugar and flavour
Frozen sweetened fruit juice or purée, with **no milk or cream**
A good choice for guests who avoid dairy. Check for other allergens.

ul: Keep ice cream and sorbet in the freezer at about **-18 °C or colder**, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.
Scoop with a clean scoop dipped in hot water and wiped. Make neat balls or a **quenelle** (a smooth oval shaped with two spoons).
**Ice cream that has melted must not be refrozen**: throw it away. Refreezing lets germs grow and spoils the texture.
On a buffet, set out frozen desserts in small amounts in a chilled bowl or on ice, and bring more from the freezer as needed.
Jamaican flavours such as soursop, mango, coconut and rum and raisin are popular with guests.

**Fruit salad**: cut fruit evenly with a clean sharp knife on a clean board. Cut apple and banana turn brown fast, so toss them in a little **lime or lemon juice**. Add **banana** at the very last minute, because it goes soft and brown quickly.
Choose ripe, fresh, undamaged tropical fruit in season: mango, pineapple, papaya, watermelon, passion fruit, star apple, naseberry.
Wash all fruit before cutting. Chill the salad and serve cold.
**Poached fruit and compote**: fruit cooked gently in syrup. Cool and chill.
Fruit can be served with ice cream, cream or a coulis.

blocks.note: Jamaica's markets give a wide choice of fruit in season. A villa kitchen that buys local ripe fruit gets better flavour and a lower cost than imported fruit, and guests enjoy tasting local varieties.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Dessert
Main ingredients
How it is made
rows: Grated sweet potato, coconut milk, brown sugar, spices (nutmeg, cinnamon), vanilla, sometimes raisins and a little flour
Mixed to a thick batter, poured into a greased tin and baked until set and golden, with a soft custard-like top. Cool before cutting.
Short pastry; grated coconut cooked with brown sugar, nutmeg and ginger
Pastry case pinched round the edge, filled with the thick, cooled filling and baked until golden.
Cooked in sugar syrup until sticky, spooned out and left to set; some are coloured pink.
Usually cornmeal or grated sweet potato or banana, coconut milk, sugar and spices
Wrapped in banana leaf and boiled.
Bread, eggs, milk or coconut milk, sugar, raisins, spices, sometimes rum
Baked in a dish until set; served hot with custard sauce.
Cornmeal, coconut milk, sugar, spices, raisins
Coconut and ginger; tamarind and sugar
Boiled sugar sweets: hot sugar burns, so take care.

ul: Check the Centre's standard recipe for exact amounts and cooking times.
Label the allergens: wheat, milk, eggs, and any nuts.
Tell the guests what each dessert is. Many visitors are curious about Jamaican dishes and enjoy a short explanation, such as what the dessert is made of and how it is cooked.

blocks.h: Making a bread pudding with custard sauce for a villa dinner

flow: Plan the timing, check for allergies, weigh the ingredients
Butter a baking dish; cut the bread into cubes or slices
Mix the eggs, milk, sugar, raisins, vanilla and spices
Pour over the bread and leave a few minutes to soak
Bake at the heat the recipe says, until set and golden
While it bakes, make the crème anglaise
Cut equal portions with a portion guide; plate warm with the sauce and a garnish
Wipe the rim; serve at once

blocks.note: A villa dinner is often served in one sitting, so a hot dessert and a sauce must be ready together. Make the sauce first and keep it warm (not boiling) in a bain-marie, and bake the pudding to finish just before service.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: The plate must be **clean, the right size and the right temperature**: **chilled** for cold desserts such as ice cream and mousse, **warm** for hot desserts such as bread pudding.
Follow the standard recipe for the portion, so every guest gets the same.
The main item is the focus: often placed slightly **off-centre**, with the sauce, garnish and accompaniment arranged around it.
Use contrast of **colour** (white cream with bright mango coulis), **texture** (soft mousse with a crisp tuile) and **height**.
Everything on the plate must be **edible** and match the flavour of the dessert: fresh mango slices and a mint leaf suit a mango mousse.
Do not overload the plate: some clear space looks neat.
**Wipe sauce drips off the rim** with a clean, damp cloth before the plate leaves the kitchen.
Dust icing sugar **just before service**.
Put hot and cold parts together at the last moment, such as warm pudding and ice cream.

head: Garnish
Use
rows: Fresh fruit slices, berries, mint leaf
Crisp contrast with ice cream and mousse.
Texture; **check** that it is nut-free and not used where coconut is a concern.
**Keep off the plate of a guest with a nut allergy.**

ul: Use a **portion marker or guide** to cut cakes, tarts and puddings into slices of equal size.
Use a scoop or a measure for ice cream, cream and sauce.
Equal portions make the dessert fair, keep the cost under control and look neat.
Set out **cream desserts in small amounts** and top up from the fridge often, so that they stay cold and safe and look fresh.
Use ice or a chilled display under cream desserts and frozen desserts.
Cover desserts when guests are not serving; use clean serving spoons for each dish and label allergens.
Do not put fresh food on top of old food in a dish. Replace the dish.

head: Dessert
Storage
rows: Mousse and set desserts made the day before
Covered, labelled with the date, and chilled at 5 °C or below.
At 5 °C or below, or as the Centre's food safety plan says.
Freezer at about -18 °C; never refreeze melted ice cream.

blocks.p: Label everything with the **name and the date** (and allergens), and use stock in date order: first in, first out. Throw out leftovers that have stood at room temperature.

ul: Switch off and unplug the mixer; wash, rinse, sanitise and dry the bowls, whisks and piping bags.
Clean work surfaces by scraping, washing with detergent, rinsing, sanitising and drying.
Report faulty equipment, low stock and accidents.
I can plan a dessert course with a mise en place and a time plan.
I can explain hygiene rules and the Food Handler's Permit.
I can name safe temperatures for cream desserts, ice cream and the danger zone.
I can handle eggs safely and explain why pasteurised egg is used in uncooked desserts.
I can find allergens in desserts and prepare a safe dessert for a guest with a nut allergy or who eats no gluten.
I can use mixers, ovens and hot sugar safely.
I can whip cream for piping and say what goes wrong if I whip it too long.
I can make a meringue and say why the sugar goes in gradually and the bowl must be grease-free.
I can fold in gently to keep the air.
I can use leaf gelatine correctly and say which fruit stops it setting.
I can name a setting agent suitable for vegetarians.
I can make crème anglaise, test it on the back of a spoon and avoid curdling.
I can explain why baked custards cook in a bain-marie.
I can melt chocolate safely and say what makes it seize.
I can make a coulis and pass it through a sieve.
I can handle ice cream and sorbet safely.
I can prepare fruit salad and stop browning.
I can make Jamaican desserts such as sweet potato pudding and gizzada.
I can plate a dessert neatly with a clean rim and the right garnish.
I can portion, store, label and serve desserts, and clean down.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I chill the plate so that the ice cream does not melt before it reaches the guest.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Having everything prepared and in its place before you start.
A container of hot water used to cook custards gently or melt chocolate.
A smooth sauce of puréed, sieved fruit.
A smooth oval shape of ice cream or mousse made with two spoons.
A setting agent made from animal collagen.
A plant-based setting agent made from seaweed.
A natural substance in fresh pineapple, papaya and kiwi that stops gelatine setting.
A light dessert of fruit or chocolate with whipped cream folded in.
Whipped cream or egg white that holds a shape but the tip folds over.
Whipped cream or egg white that stands up in a point.
Whisked egg whites and sugar, dried in a low oven.
Gently combining a light mix into a heavier one without losing air.
A pouring custard sauce; coats the back of a spoon.
When egg in a custard scrambles or a mix splits.
Cornflour mixed with cold liquid, used to thicken.
When chocolate turns thick, dull and lumpy after contact with water.
Sugar heated until golden; very hot.
A frozen dessert of fruit and sugar, with no milk or cream.
A thin, crisp, curved biscuit used as a garnish.
Egg that has been heat-treated to make it safe to use uncooked.
A substance that can cause a harmful reaction in some people.
Food in which germs grow quickly, such as cream and custard.
Baking a pastry case empty before it is filled.

c1.title: A villa dinner for ten in Runaway Bay
c1.text: Chef Colleen is planning the dessert for a villa dinner for ten guests in Runaway Bay at 7:30 p.m. One guest has a severe tree nut allergy and another eats no gluten. The menu is a mango mousse in glasses with a crisp biscuit and mango coulis. Trainee Orlando suggests making everything at 6:30 p.m. so it is fresh. The biscuits are bought in and the label says 'may contain nuts'.

c2.title: A jelly that did not set in Ocho Rios
c2.text: At a hotel kitchen in Ocho Rios, trainee Simone makes a tropical fruit jelly with leaf gelatine for a buffet. She boils the dissolved gelatine in the pan to make sure it melts, and adds chopped fresh papaya and kiwi fruit. Six hours later the jelly is still runny. A guest at the buffet asks whether the dessert is suitable for a vegetarian.

c3.title: Custards for a hotel lunch in Kingston
c3.text: In a hotel kitchen in Kingston, trainee Keron makes crème anglaise to go with a hot apple tart, and a crème caramel for the cold buffet. He cooks the sauce over a high heat and stops stirring while he answers a question. The sauce looks lumpy. For the crème caramel, he puts the dishes straight on an oven tray with no water, in a hot oven. The caramel custards come out full of tiny holes.

c4.title: Meringue nests at the Centre in Montego Bay
c4.text: Trainees at the Centre's kitchen in Montego Bay make meringue nests with whipped cream, fruit and mango coulis for a hotel lunch. Pauline cracks an egg and a little yolk gets into the whites; she adds all the sugar in one go. Her meringue will not whip. Jerome whips the cream for ten minutes while he cuts fruit, and it becomes grainy. He fills the baked nests with cream at 9:00 a.m. for a 1:00 p.m. lunch. The nests are soft and sticky by lunch.

c5.title: A wedding dessert table in Black River
c5.text: A wedding at a venue in Black River has a dessert table with a cream gateau, bowls of ice cream, a tray of sweet potato pudding and a coulis. The ice cream is put out in large tubs at 11:00 a.m. for a 2:00 p.m. reception. By the time the cake is cut it has melted into a puddle. The caterer wants to refreeze the melted ice cream. Waiter Devon notices drips of sauce on the plate rims, and a guest asks if the pudding has nuts.

questions.q: The biscuits are labelled 'may contain nuts'. What should Chef Colleen do for the guest with the nut allergy?
o: Serve the biscuits, since nuts are not on the ingredient list
Pick out the biscuits that look plain and leave the rest
Leave the biscuit off and use a garnish that is safe
Ask the guest whether a small amount would be acceptable
questions.why: A 'may contain nuts' warning means the biscuit is not safe for a guest with a severe nut allergy. Use a garnish that is clearly free from nuts, such as fresh fruit, and keep the dessert apart.

questions.q: What is the safest way to prepare the allergy-free desserts?
o: Make them first on a cleaned surface with clean tools
Make them last, using the same bowls as the other desserts
Make them with the others on the same board, side by side
Make them after the rest, then wipe the bowls with a cloth
questions.why: Cleaning first, using clean tools and keeping the dessert covered and apart, stops traces of nuts or gluten from getting in. Serve it straight to the right guest and tell the guest what it is.

questions.q: Why is Orlando's plan to make the mousse at 6:30 p.m. a poor one?
o: Mousse has to be eaten the day it is made
Mousse is better if it is served at room temperature
Mousse cannot be made with mango in the evening
Mousse needs several hours in the fridge to set
questions.why: Gelatine takes hours to set. A mousse for a 7:30 p.m. dinner should be made hours ahead, or the day before, covered, labelled and chilled.

questions.q: Which dessert would suit the guest who eats no gluten?
o: A bread pudding with raisins and spice
A fruit salad with mango and mint
A crisp biscuit with whipped cream
A wheat flour sponge with a coulis
questions.why: Fruit contains no gluten. Bread pudding, biscuits and sponge are made from wheat. Always check labels and recipes, because gluten can hide in sauces and chocolate.

questions.q: Why is Simone's jelly still runny?
o: She boiled the gelatine, and fresh papaya and kiwi break it down
The fruit was cut into pieces that were too large to set evenly
The jelly stood at room temperature for the first hour of setting
She soaked the leaf gelatine in cold water before melting it
questions.why: Boiling weakens gelatine, and fresh papaya and kiwi contain enzymes that break it down. Melt gelatine gently, and use cooked or canned fruit in a jelly.

questions.q: Which fruit could Simone add to a gelatine jelly without stopping it from setting?
o: Fresh papaya
Fresh kiwi fruit
Fresh pineapple
Fresh mango
questions.why: Mango does not have the enzymes that stop gelatine from setting. Fresh papaya, kiwi and pineapple do, unless they are cooked or canned.

questions.q: The guest asks if the jelly is suitable for a vegetarian. What is the correct answer?
o: Yes, as jelly is made from fruit juice only
Yes, if the gelatine has been boiled first
No, as gelatine comes from animals; agar would suit
No, as vegetarians cannot eat any fruit that has been cooked
questions.why: Gelatine is made from animal collagen, so it is not suitable for vegetarians. Agar, made from seaweed, is a plant-based setting agent.

questions.q: Why does Keron's custard sauce look lumpy?
o: The egg scrambled: the heat was too high and he stopped stirring
The milk was heated with the vanilla for too long a time
The sauce was strained into a cold bowl a little too soon
The sugar was added to the yolks before the milk was heated
questions.why: Egg sets and scrambles above a gentle heat. Cook crème anglaise over a low heat, stirring all the time, and never boil it.

questions.q: How can Keron tell when a good crème anglaise is cooked?
o: It is as thin as milk and runs straight off the spoon
It coats the back of a spoon, and a line drawn stays clear
It begins to bubble gently at the edge of the pan
It forms a skin on the top as soon as it cools down
questions.why: A cooked crème anglaise thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon. If it bubbles, it has boiled and may curdle.

questions.q: Why are crème caramels cooked in a bain-marie?
o: The water cooks the custard faster than a dry oven would
The water stops the caramel in the dish from setting hard
The gentle, even heat lets the custard set smoothly
The water makes the custards turn out of the dishes more easily
questions.why: A tray of hot water keeps the heat gentle and even, so the egg sets smoothly. With no water in a hot oven the custard overheats and bubbles, leaving holes.

questions.q: After cooling, how should the crème caramels be kept before the buffet?
o: Covered, labelled and chilled at 5 °C or below
On the bench, covered with a cloth, until service
In the warm cupboard so that the caramel stays liquid
Uncovered in the fridge so that they set faster
questions.why: Egg custard is a high-risk food. Keep it covered and chilled, with a label showing the date, and use it as the Centre's food safety plan says.

questions.q: Why will Pauline's meringue not whip?
o: Yolk fat stopped the foaming, and the sugar went in early
She used cold eggs, which do not whip as well as warm ones
She used caster sugar, when the recipe needs icing sugar
She cracked the egg too early in the day and let it stand
questions.why: Even a little yolk (fat) stops egg whites foaming. The sugar goes in gradually once the whites are foamy, not all at once.

questions.q: What has happened to Jerome's cream?
o: It was too cold to whip properly, so it split
It is over-whipped and has begun to turn into butter
It has taken in too much air from the whisk
It was whipped with too little sugar in it
questions.why: Cream whipped too long goes grainy and starts to separate into butter. Stop at firm peaks for piping, and watch it all the time.

questions.q: Why are the meringue nests soft and sticky by lunch?
o: They were filled with cream four hours too early
They were baked in an oven that was too cool
They were piped with too much sugar in the mix
They were taken out of the oven while still warm
questions.why: Cream and fruit put moisture into the dry meringue and make it soft. Fill the nests close to service and keep the cream chilled.

questions.q: Pauline's mango coulis tastes very sweet and flat. What is the best fix?
o: Stir in a little lime juice
Stir in a spoonful more sugar
Add a pinch of cornflour
Cook it for ten minutes
questions.why: Acid balances sweetness and lifts the flavour of fruit. Taste the coulis and adjust: lime juice if too sweet, sugar if too sharp.

questions.q: What is the right thing to do with the melted ice cream?
o: Refreeze it quickly in a clean container
Throw it away and never refreeze it
Keep it in the fridge and serve it as a sauce
Stir it and put it back in the freezer for later
questions.why: Melted ice cream has been warm enough for germs to grow, and freezing does not kill them. It must be thrown away.

questions.q: How should the ice cream have been served at the reception?
o: In large tubs on the table, so that guests could serve themselves
In small amounts in a chilled bowl on ice, topped up as needed
In a deep tub in the kitchen, scooped out only when asked for
In a sealed box, brought out only when the cake is cut
questions.why: Small amounts on ice stay cold and safe, and the staff top up from the freezer as needed. Large tubs left out for hours melt and are unsafe.

questions.q: The sweet potato pudding is to be served hot with a scoop of ice cream. When should Devon add the ice cream?
o: At the last moment, just before the plate goes out
As soon as the pudding is cut, so that it stays cool
Ten minutes early, so that the two can blend together
Before the pudding is warmed through, to chill the plate
questions.why: Ice cream melts quickly on a hot dessert. Put hot and cold parts together at the last moment, so that the dessert reaches the guest at its best.

questions.q: A trainee is making caramel and must add a little liquid to the golden sugar. What is the safest way to do it?
o: A little at a time, standing back, because it spits
All at once, so the caramel stops cooking quickly
Leaning over the pan, so the mixing can be watched
With the pan held in one hand and a whisk in the other
questions.why: Hot sugar is far hotter than boiling water, and liquid added to it spits and steams. Add it slowly, with a long spoon and the handle turned in, and stand back.

questions.q: A guest has asked for a cold dessert with no dairy. Which of these suits them best?
o: A mango sorbet made with fruit and sugar only
A soursop ice cream made with fresh cream
A chocolate mousse with whipped cream folded in
A bread pudding served with crème anglaise
questions.why: Sorbet has no milk or cream, so it suits a guest who avoids dairy. Ice cream, mousse and custard sauce all contain milk or cream. Still check every ingredient label.
